description: Genesis 1 and 2 accounts of creation, imago Dei, stewardship and different Christian beliefs about creation.
content_html:
Two Accounts, One Message

The Bible opens with two distinct accounts of creation in Genesis 1 and Genesis 2. Catholic teaching does not require these to be read as competing stories or as a scientific textbook. Instead, the Church understands them as complementary theological accounts that reveal truths about God, the world and human beings. Genesis 1 is a majestic, structured poem in which God creates in six days and rests on the seventh. Genesis 2 is a more intimate narrative focusing on the garden, the first human, and the gift of companionship. Together they form the foundation for the Catholic understanding of creation.

Key Fact

Genesis 1 reveals that God is the source of all existence, that creation is deliberately ordered and good, and that human beings are made in God’s image (imago Dei). Genesis 2 reveals that humanity is formed from the earth yet breathed into life by God — a blend of the material and the spiritual.

Genesis 1 and the Nature of God

In Genesis 1, God creates the world through speech alone: “And God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light.” This emphasises God’s absolute power and sovereignty — nothing exists independently of his will. Each stage of creation is declared “good”, and the whole is declared “very good” (Genesis 1:31). For Catholics, this teaches that the material world is not evil or fallen by nature — it is a gift from a generous Creator. The regular rhythm of six days of work and one day of rest (the Sabbath) models the pattern of human life and later becomes the basis for keeping Sunday holy in Catholic practice.

The pinnacle of Genesis 1 is the creation of humanity on the sixth day: “God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). The concept of imago Dei — being made in God’s image — is central to Catholic anthropology. It means that every human being possesses inherent dignity that cannot be taken away, regardless of their social status, nationality or actions.

Genesis 2 and the Dignity of Human Beings

Genesis 2 presents a more personal creation narrative. The LORD God forms the human from the dust of the ground and “breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living being” (Genesis 2:7). This dual origin — from the earth and from God’s own breath — captures the Catholic understanding of human beings as both physical and spiritual creatures. The body is not a prison for the soul; both together constitute the human person.

The creation of the woman as a partner “suitable for him” (Genesis 2:18) establishes the dignity of both sexes as equally made in God’s image. Catholic teaching, drawing on Genesis 2, insists that neither man nor woman is superior — both reflect the image of God fully. The Catholic Catechism, summarising this teaching, states that human beings are the only creatures God has willed for their own sake.

Christians hold a range of views on the relationship between Genesis and modern science. Creationism (literal six-day creation) is held by some evangelical Protestant Christians, who read Genesis as historical fact. Catholic teaching since at least the papacy of Pius XII has explicitly rejected a rigid literal reading; the Church affirms that the theory of evolution is compatible with belief in God as Creator, provided one upholds that human souls are directly created by God.

Theistic evolution is the position held by most Catholic theologians and by the majority of mainstream Protestant denominations. God is the ultimate cause of the universe’s existence; the scientific account of how life developed is not in competition with the theological account of why it exists. This approach allows Catholics to accept the findings of cosmology and evolutionary biology while affirming that the universe is God’s creation and that every human being has a unique, God-given dignity.

Stewardship of Creation

Genesis 1 calls human beings to “have dominion” over the earth (Genesis 1:28). Catholic teaching interprets this not as a licence to exploit creation but as a call to stewardship — caring for the world as trustees on behalf of God. This position was reinforced by Pope Francis in Laudato Si’ (2015), a major teaching document on care for the environment, which described the earth as “our common home” and argued that the exploitation of natural resources is both an ecological and a moral problem. The document’s argument is grounded directly in the Genesis vision of creation as good and humanity as its responsible guardians.

Catholic communities across Britain today engage in environmental action inspired by this theology: parish eco-groups, fair-trade campaigns, and support for organisations such as CAFOD’s climate justice work all connect the Genesis mandate to present-day responsibility. Orthodox Christianity similarly emphasises creation care, viewing the earth as a sacrament — a means of encountering God. Protestant Christians may emphasise the dominion mandate differently, though many mainstream Protestant denominations now share the Catholic emphasis on responsible stewardship.

A common student error is to interpret “made in God’s image” as a physical resemblance — as if Genesis is claiming God has a body like ours. Catholic theology has consistently interpreted imago Dei as referring to the spiritual and moral capacities that humans share with God: reason, free will, conscience, the capacity for love and relationship. God is not a physical being; the ‘image’ is about what makes humans unique among creatures — their spiritual dimension and moral responsibility. This is a mark-scheme-distinguishing answer.

Key Fact

Imago Dei (Genesis 1:27) means every human being is made in God’s image and therefore possesses inherent dignity and worth. For Catholic teaching this is the foundation of human rights, the condemnation of slavery, abortion, murder and euthanasia, and the call to treat every person as an end in themselves, never merely as a means.
exam_tip_html:
For the 6-mark Explain question on creation, you must name a sacred text. Genesis 1:27 (“God created mankind in his own image”) is the most valuable single verse you can cite: it establishes imago Dei, grounds human dignity, and supports multiple developed reasons. Always name the chapter and verse — “Genesis 1” alone is acceptable but “Genesis 1:27” demonstrates precision that rewards top-band answers.

A very common error on creation questions is treating Genesis 1 and Genesis 2 as contradictory. The exam mark scheme rewards students who explain that they are complementary theological accounts. Catholic teaching affirms that belief in God as creator is compatible with the science of evolution (theistic evolution) — knowing this contrast earns marks on a 12-mark Evaluate statement about science vs religion.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Genesis 1 and Genesis 2 are two complementary accounts of creation. Genesis 1 reveals God’s power and declares creation ‘very good’; Genesis 2 reveals the intimate creation of the human person from earth and divine breath. Catholic teaching reads both theologically, not as a scientific alternative to evolution.
  • Imago Dei (Genesis 1:27) — being made in God’s image — is the foundation of human dignity in Catholic belief. It means every human being has inherent worth, regardless of circumstance, and is the basis for Catholic social teaching on human rights.
  • Catholics understand ‘dominion’ over creation (Genesis 1:28) as stewardship — responsible care for the world as trustees on behalf of God. This teaching was developed by Pope Francis in Laudato Si’ (2015) and underpins Catholic environmental engagement today.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the Catholic understanding of imago Dei?
A) Human beings physically resemble God in appearance
B) Human beings are made in God's image, giving them special dignity and moral capacity
C) Only priests and religious leaders are made in God's image
D) The concept of imago Dei means human beings are gods themselves
practice_questions.marks: B) Human beings are made in God's image, giving them special dignity and moral capacity [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one way in which Catholic teaching interprets the command to have 'dominion' over creation (Genesis 1:28).
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for any of the following:
- As a call to stewardship / responsible care of creation on God's behalf.
- Not as a licence to exploit creation but as a duty to protect it.
- As trusteeship of the earth for future generations.
Do not accept 'control over animals' without reference to responsibility.

practice_questions.text: Explain two contrasting Christian beliefs about how to interpret the Genesis accounts of creation.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks: 2 marks per belief (1 for a brief point, 2 for a developed point).
Acceptable points include:
- Some evangelical Protestant Christians hold a creationist or literal view: the six days in Genesis 1 are literal 24-hour days and God created the world exactly as described, making the scientific theory of evolution incompatible with Christian belief.
- Catholic teaching (and most mainstream Protestant denominations) endorses theistic evolution: God created the universe and initiated its development through natural processes; the Genesis accounts are theological, not scientific, and are compatible with evolutionary biology. The soul is directly created by God.
- Some Christians read Genesis 1 and 2 as poetry or allegory, prioritising their theological message over any historical claims.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why the teaching that human beings are made in the image of God (imago Dei) is important for Catholic Christians.
In your answer you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious belief and teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two fully developed reasons with precise theological knowledge; named source cited and integrated into the explanation (e.g. Genesis 1:27, Pope Francis's Laudato Si'); both reasons clearly connected to significance for Catholic belief or practice.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two reasons present, accurate, source present but undeveloped; one reason more developed than the other.
Developing (2 marks): One reason developed or two briefly stated; limited or no source reference.
Emerging (1 mark): A basic relevant point; no source; generic rather than Catholic-specific.

Acceptable points include:
- Imago Dei (Genesis 1:27) establishes that every human being has inherent dignity that cannot be removed — this means Catholics must oppose anything that degrades or destroys human life, from slavery to abortion, because to harm a person made in God's image is to dishonour God himself.
- It is the theological foundation of Catholic Social Teaching — the Catechism teaches that humans are the only creatures God has willed for their own sake; this grounds the Church's work for human rights, justice and the poor.
- Pope Francis's Laudato Si' (2015) connects imago Dei to environmental responsibility: because human beings uniquely bear God's image, they also uniquely bear responsibility for the rest of creation.

practice_questions.text:
'The Genesis accounts of creation are no longer relevant in a scientific age.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Catholic teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Balanced evaluation; Catholic position on theistic evolution explained accurately; creationist position acknowledged; non-religious/scientific view given; source references (Genesis 1:27, Laudato Si'); sub-tradition contrasts (Catholic vs evangelical Protestant); justified conclusion.
Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides present; source cited; conclusion reached but not fully justified.
Developing (4-6 marks): One-sided or both sides briefly stated; limited source reference.
Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic points, no sources, no conclusion.

Arguments in support:
- Modern cosmology (the Big Bang) and evolutionary biology provide comprehensive scientific accounts of the origin of the universe and life; some argue the Genesis accounts add nothing to this understanding.
- Creationist readings of Genesis have been shown to be scientifically inaccurate; if the text is not literally true, critics argue it loses its authority.
- In a secular society, basing ethics on an ancient text may seem less persuasive than grounding them in reason and human rights law.

Arguments against:
- Catholic teaching holds that Genesis answers a different question from science: not 'how' but 'why' the world exists and what human beings are for. Science cannot tell us that human beings have dignity — theology can.
- The concept of imago Dei (Genesis 1:27) continues to underpin Catholic Social Teaching, human rights advocacy, and environmental responsibility (Laudato Si', 2015) — its practical relevance is demonstrably alive.
- Theistic evolution shows the Genesis accounts and science are compatible; the Church has formally endorsed evolution while maintaining that God is the ultimate creator and source of the human soul.

Conclusion: Candidates may reasonably argue that Genesis remains highly relevant as a theological and ethical framework, or that its relevance depends on whether it is read literally or symbolically. A justified conclusion must state a reasoned preference.

practice_questions.text: Sister Maria, a Catholic Religious Education teacher at a secondary school in Birmingham, explains to her class why the Church teaches that every person has equal dignity. Give two reasons she might give, based on Catholic teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for each valid point (up to 2 marks total).
Acceptable points include:
- Every human being is made in God's image (imago Dei, Genesis 1:27), giving each person inherent dignity regardless of status.
- Genesis 2 describes both man and woman as formed by God and breathed into life — neither is superior.
- Catholic teaching holds that God wills every person for their own sake, not as a means to an end.

knowledge_checks.q: What does the Latin phrase imago Dei mean?
Which Catholic understanding of creation holds that God created the universe but used natural processes such as evolution?
Genesis 1:27 states that God created mankind in his own _____, male and female he created them.
In Genesis 2:7, God forms the human from the dust of the ground and breathes into his nostrils the _____ of life.
Match each concept to its correct description:
right: The teaching that human beings are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27)
The responsible care of God's creation on behalf of God
The view that God created the universe but used natural processes to develop life

flashcard_questions.a: Latin for 'in the image of God' — the teaching that every human has inherent dignity (Genesis 1:27).

flashcard_questions.q: What does Genesis 1 teach about the nature of God?
flashcard_questions.a: God is the all-powerful creator who speaks creation into existence and declares it 'very good'.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Genesis 2:7 reveal about human beings?
flashcard_questions.a: Humans are formed from earth and breathed into life by God — both material and spiritual creatures.
The belief that Genesis is literally true and God created the world in six 24-hour days.
The view that God created the universe and used natural processes such as evolution to develop life.
The responsibility to care for God's creation as trustees on behalf of God, not to exploit it.

flashcard_questions.q: Which papal document (2015) developed Catholic teaching on care for the environment?
flashcard_questions.a: Laudato Si' by Pope Francis — described the earth as 'our common home' and grounded care for it in Genesis.

flashcard_questions.q: How does Catholic teaching interpret 'dominion' over creation in Genesis 1:28?
flashcard_questions.a: As stewardship — responsible care and guardianship, not exploitation.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Genesis 2 add to the Genesis 1 creation account?
flashcard_questions.a: An intimate narrative of God personally forming the human, emphasising relationship and companionship.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does imago Dei matter for Catholic teaching on human rights?
flashcard_questions.a: Because every person bears God's image, all have inherent dignity — the foundation of Catholic Social Teaching.

glossary_terms.definition: Latin phrase meaning 'in the image of God', describing the special dignity of human beings in Catholic teaching (Genesis 1:27).
The responsible management and care of God's creation, acting as caretakers on behalf of God.
The belief that the Genesis accounts of creation are literally true and that God created the world in six 24-hour days.
The view that God created the universe and initiated its development, but used natural processes such as evolution to do so.
The seventh day of creation in Genesis 1, on which God rested; the basis of the Jewish and Christian practice of a weekly day of rest.
A major teaching document by Pope Francis (2015) on care for the environment, grounding environmental responsibility in the Genesis account of creation.

hero_image_caption: Catholic teaching reads Genesis 1 and 2 as complementary theological accounts revealing that the world is God's gift and every human being bears the divine image.
